claims.text: Actively learned moment tensor potentials can be parameterized using ab initio training data.
Active learning can target ab initio configurations iteratively for training the surrogate potential.
Combining an actively learned moment tensor potential with thermodynamic integration can faithfully calculate both solid and liquid free energies near fusion.
The proposed framework can capture vibrational contributions to free energy.
The proposed framework can capture anharmonic contributions to free energy.
The proposed framework can capture electron–vibration or electron–phonon contributions to free energy.
Moment tensor potentials represent the local atomic configurations needed for the proposed free-energy calculations.
Vibrational entropy can contribute to the thermodynamic stabilization of an alloy.
Using the surrogate potential substantially reduces the number of expensive ab initio molecular-dynamics steps required.
The reduction in ab initio sampling preserves the key entropy contributions needed for accurate fusion free energies.
The proposed method will provide an order-of-magnitude speedup over explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will outperform TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties will deviate by less than 5% from reference results.
The initial applicability of the method is expected to cover elemental and binary systems near their melting temperatures.
Extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys may require additional potential retraining or calibration.
A comparison of solid–liquid free-energy differences, latent heat, heat capacity, and vibrational entropy against explicit ab initio and experimental benchmarks can test fidelity.
A deviation greater than approximately 5% in the benchmarked free energies or derived observables is defined to falsify the fidelity claim.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome asserts improved performance over TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems, but the stated applicability is restricted initially to elemental and binary systems and performance in multicomponent high-entropy alloys is explicitly described as uncertain.
